newsitem.title: JAPAN: Dlr seen firm above 116 yen but top-heavy in Asia.
newsitem.headline: Dlr seen firm above 116 yen but top-heavy in Asia.

text.p: The dollar is expected to be firm above 116 yen during Asian trading time on Wednesday after overnight gains on political uncertainty in Europe and worries about European monetary union, dealers said.
Bids from Japanese investors and importers are likely to emerge below 116 yen, supporting the greenback, but the dollar's topside remains heavy with exporter offers near 117 yen, they added.
"Amid uncertainty on European economic and monetary union (EMU), it is easy to go for dollar purchases amid the current sentiment," a trust bank dealer said.
He said importers who had failed to buy dollars near the 112-113 yen level previously may decide to buy dollars below 116 yen, making the greenback's downside solid.

But a city bank dealer said exporters are expected to remain eager to sell dollars near 117 yen. "They were said to have sold dollars for yen yesterday. Their offers will keep the greenback's topside heavy today as well," he added.

Dealers said they will watch closely for possible comments on Japanese interest rates by Bank of Japan Governor Yasuo Matsushita at his regular news conference at 0600 GMT, but they said the impact on currencies may be limited.

"Japanese interest rates have had an upward bias recently, so even if he (Matsushita) says something on rates, it may not push the dollar down sharply below 115 yen. But we are still paying close attention to his news conference," the city bank dealer said.

In New York, investors bought the greenback for its safe haven status as they digested news of the unexpected lead by left-wing parties in the first round of French parliamentary elections on Sunday and Monday's resignation announcement by conservative Prime Minister Alain Juppe.

One of Juppe's potential successors, National Assembly Speaker Philippe Seguin, sent the dollar to session highs by saying he favours looser fiscal criteria and a larger pool of entrants in the first wave of EMU. Seguin's remarks, to be published on Wednesday in the weekly magazine L'Express, were reported by wire services at the U.S. midday.
"It is up to European markets now. If (European) traders adopt a dollar-buying sentiment, it could push the greenback higher," the city bank dealer said.
